subject: chemistry-2
question: A buffer has its greatest capacity to resist pH change under which condition?

options.text: When the weak acid has been nearly completely titrated
When the conjugate base greatly exceeds the weak acid
When the solution pH is at least two units above the pKa
When the concentrations of weak acid and conjugate base are equal

explanation:
Buffer capacity peaks when [A-] equals [HA], because equal reservoirs absorb added acid and added base equally well. That condition corresponds to pH equal to pKa, since log 1 is 0 in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. For the phosphate pair with a physiologic pKa near 6.8, maximal buffering therefore occurs at pH 6.8, conveniently close to intracellular pH. Each of the other three conditions describes a ratio far from 1:1: nearly complete titration of the weak acid leaves almost no HA to neutralize added base, a large excess of conjugate base leaves almost no HA for the same reason, and a pH two or more units above the pKa means the base-to-acid ratio is at least 100:1. In every one of those cases one reservoir is nearly exhausted and pH becomes highly sensitive to further additions; useful buffering is generally limited to about one pH unit on either side of the pKa.

ELI-10: Picture a seesaw with sandbags on both ends. With equal loads, removing one bag from either side barely tilts it. If one end is nearly empty, a single bag slams it down. Equal amounts of acid and base is the balanced seesaw, and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation tells you where that happens: when the two are equal their ratio is 1, the logarithm of 1 is 0, so the pH sits exactly at the pKa. For phosphate that balance point is pH 6.8.
